passages.title: Are We Using Up the Earth's Resources?
passages.subtitle: Facing overconsumption, deforestation, and the move toward smarter conservation
paragraphs: Every house, smartphone, and meal depends on natural resources taken from the Earth, including wood, clean water, metals, and fertile soil. For centuries, people acted as if the planet's supplies were endless. Today, however, scientists warn that our Earth is finite, and rapid overconsumption is pushing many vital supplies close to their limits.

One clear example of resource depletion is deforestation. Every year, millions of hectares of tropical forest are cleared to raise cattle, grow palm oil, or supply timber for furniture and paper. Cutting down ancient forests does not just destroy trees; it also removes homes for countless animals and reduces biodiversity, while releasing carbon stored in the wood.

Underground minerals are also under heavy strain. Metals such as copper, lithium, and cobalt are essential for smartphones, cables, and electric car batteries. Because global demand has risen sharply, mining companies have to dig deeper mines that use huge amounts of water and energy. Some experts warn that if extraction continues at current speeds, easy-to-reach supplies of several key metals could run out of affordable ore within a few decades.

Oceans are feeling the pressure as well. Modern fishing fleets equipped with giant nets and satellite trackers can catch enormous amounts of fish in a single trip. When fish are caught faster than they can reproduce, fish stocks collapse, threatening both marine food chains and the livelihoods of small coastal fishermen.

To slow this decline, environmental groups promote practical conservation and a 'circular economy'. Instead of digging up fresh materials for every new product, factories can recover copper and gold from old electronics, while builders can reuse timber and steel from demolished offices. On an individual level, buying durable items, sharing tools with neighbours, and wasting less food can significantly reduce the pressure on our planet's limited stores.

passages.title: Fuel Prices and the Environment
passages.subtitle: Can higher fuel taxes reduce private car use fairly?
paragraphs: Private petrol cars are one of the biggest sources of urban air pollution and carbon emissions. To fight climate change, many economists suggest raising the fuel tax on petrol and diesel. The basic idea is simple: when filling up a tank becomes expensive, governments can discourage unnecessary car trips and motivate drivers to choose cleaner ways to travel.

Evidence from several European cities shows that higher petrol prices do change travel habits over time. When fuel costs jump, commuters are more likely to share rides with colleagues, walk for short errands, or buy smaller, fuel-saving cars. In addition, the extra tax money collected at petrol stations can be spent on improving buses, trams, and train lines.

However, raising fuel prices is politically unpopular and can hurt low-income households unfairly. Wealthy drivers can easily absorb an extra ten dollars at the pump or switch to expensive electric vehicles. By contrast, rural workers, nurses on night shifts, and delivery drivers often live in areas with poor bus services, meaning they have no choice but to keep driving older petrol cars while paying a larger share of their weekly wages.

Because of these fairness concerns, transport experts warn that fuel taxes alone are not enough. Before making petrol more expensive, cities must first provide affordable alternatives. Investing in frequent, clean, and reliable public transport—with low-cost monthly passes—gives commuters a real reason to leave their car keys at home.

Governments can also use positive incentives rather than just penalties. In Norway, buyers of electric vehicles enjoy zero purchase tax, free ferry crossings, and cheaper parking, helping electric cars become the top-selling vehicles in the country. Other nations offer trade-in rebates that help poorer families swap old polluting cars for clean second-hand models or electric bicycles.

passages.title: Fresh Water: A Limited Resource
passages.subtitle: Why water scarcity is growing—and how technology and conservation can help
paragraphs: 1 Although water covers more than seventy percent of our planet's surface, almost all of it is salty seawater. Less than three percent of Earth's water is fresh, and most of that is locked inside glaciers or deep underground. As a result, clean drinkable water is a surprisingly scarce treasure that billions of people cannot take for granted.

2 Today, water scarcity is worsening rapidly due to two main pressures: rapid population growth and climate change. Growing megacities need vast daily supplies for drinking, washing, and power stations. At the same time, severe drought is drying up rivers and reservoirs across parts of Africa, Asia, and southern Europe, leaving taps dry during hot summer months.

3 Surprisingly, household taps account for only a small fraction of global water use. Roughly seventy percent of all fresh water goes to agriculture—mostly for farm irrigation—while factories and mining use another twenty percent. Worse still, untreated factory waste and farm chemicals pollute many remaining rivers, making water unsafe to drink without costly cleaning.

4 To secure future supplies, engineers are turning to smart technology. Coastal desert nations such as Israel and the United Arab Emirates rely heavily on desalination—a process that removes salt from seawater to produce fresh drinking water. Meanwhile, modern wastewater treatment plants in Singapore clean used city water so thoroughly that it can be reused safely by factories and even added back to drinking reservoirs.

5 Yet high-tech plants have limits: desalination uses large amounts of electricity and leaves salty waste behind that can harm coastal sea life. Therefore, water experts stress that upgrading leaky city pipes and changing farm habits are just as important. Drip irrigation, which delivers water drop by drop directly to plant roots, can cut farm water waste by half compared with open spraying.

6 Every citizen also plays a part in helping to conserve water. Fixing dripping taps, taking shorter showers, and collecting rainwater for gardens may seem small on their own, but across a city of five million people, those habits save millions of litres every week. Treating fresh water as a precious, limited resource is the only way to guarantee enough for everyone.
